known_facts_book1: Is first only an extremely small voice close to Alice's ear in the railway carriage, suggesting jokes about 'horse' and 'hoarse'.
Says it knows Alice is a friend, a dear friend and an old friend, and that she won't hurt it though it is an insect.
Turns out to be a very large Gnat, about the size of a chicken, balancing on a twig and fanning her with its wings.

Names the Looking-glass insects: the Rocking-horse-fly of wood that lives on sap and sawdust, the Snap-dragon-fly of plum-pudding and holly-leaves, and the Bread-and-Butterfly whose head is a lump of sugar.
Says the Bread-and-Butterfly would die if it could not find weak tea with cream in it, and that this always happens.
Points out the wood further on where things have got no names.
Makes the joke about the governess calling 'Miss!', asks Alice to admire it, and weeps large tears when she calls it a bad one.
Sighs itself away, leaving nothing whatever to be seen on the twig.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Talks with her from the carriage to the twig, makes bad jokes at her and vanishes; she is sorry for it.

not_in_this_book: the Gnat guides Alice to the Eighth Square

known_facts_book1: Comes wandering by in the wood where things have no names, and looks at Alice with large gentle eyes without being frightened.
Asks Alice what she calls herself, and is told 'Nothing, just now'.
Says it cannot remember its own name in that place, and asks Alice to move a little further on.
Walks out of the wood with Alice's arms clasped lovingly round its soft neck.
Cries 'I'm a Fawn! and, dear me! you're a human child!' the moment they leave the wood, and darts away at full speed in alarm.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Her fellow-traveller through the nameless wood, lost the instant both remember what they are. Not an enemy — the alarm is instinct, not malice.

not_in_this_book: the Fawn speaks again after leaving the wood

known_facts_book1: Is what the White Queen becomes, her last 'better' ending in a long bleat.
Sits in an arm-chair behind the counter of a little dark shop, knitting and looking at Alice through a great pair of spectacles.
Tells Alice she may look in front of her and on both sides, but cannot look all round unless she has eyes at the back of her head.
Knits with fourteen pairs of needles at once, and takes up more and more until she sticks some in her hair.
Hands Alice a pair of knitting-needles that turn into oars in a little boat.
Cries 'Feather!' at Alice while she rows, warns her she will be catching a crab, and calls her a little goose.
Sells eggs at fivepence farthing for one and twopence for two, on the condition that two must both be eaten.
Refuses to put the egg into Alice's hands and sets it upright on a shelf at the far end of the shop, where it turns into Humpty Dumpty.

known_relations_book1.White Queen: The Queen she is a transformation of, in the middle of the wool-and-water chapter.
known_relations_book1.Alice: Serves her in the shop, rows with her, and sells her the egg. Brusque, never hostile.
known_relations_book1.Humpty Dumpty: The egg she sold Alice grows into him.

known_facts_book1: Puts his head in at the carriage window calling 'Tickets, please!'
Demands Alice's ticket angrily, and the chorus of voices says his time is worth a thousand pounds a minute.
Tells her she should have bought one from the engine-driver, since there was no ticket-office where she came from.
Looks at her first through a telescope, then through a microscope, then through an opera-glass.
Tells her 'You're travelling the wrong way', shuts the window and goes away.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Inspects her, finds her ticketless, and pronounces her to be going the wrong way.

not_in_this_book: the Guard throws Alice off the train

known_facts_book1: Sits next to the gentleman dressed in white paper in the railway carriage.
Shuts his eyes and says in a loud voice that Alice ought to know her way to the ticket-office even if she doesn't know her alphabet.
Has his beard caught by Alice when the carriage rises into the air to jump the brook, and the beard melts away as she touches it.

known_relations_book1.Alice: One of the passengers who takes his turn at telling her what she ought to know.

not_in_this_book: the Goat follows Alice out of the train
